title: How Hollywood’s Veterans Are Chasing Emmy History: Sally Field, Harrison Ford, Martin Short and More

body:
Awards season loves a fresh face, but this one also loves a weathered one.

	When the Television Academy announced its nominations in July, the story wasn’t about the ingenues. It was about the lifers, the character actors, the movie stars and the beloved figures we lost along the way. Voters have handed us a September ceremony where nearly every envelope could contain a piece of Emmy history.


	Harrison Ford, 84 on Emmy night, is back for Apple TV’s “Shrinking” — still chasing the first major acting trophy of a 60-year screen career. The oldest winner in the category’s history is Henry Winkler, who was 72 when he won for the first season of “Barry” in 2018. Ford would shatter that record. He would also supplant Bob Newhart — 84 when he finally won for “The Big Bang Theory” in 2013 — as the oldest man ever to win a comedy acting Emmy, by a matter of weeks.
	

	And here’s the beautiful part: If Ford doesn’t do it, Stephen Root might. The 74-year-old, nominated for the freshman horror-comedy “Widow’s Bay” after some 250 credits and zero wins, would top Winkler’s mark. Two men older than the standing record, in the same category, in the same year, is pitch perfect.


	The lead comedy actor race carries the same energy. Martin Short, 76, lands his fifth consecutive nomination for Hulu’s mystery romp “Only Murders in the Building” — his eighth acting nod overall, but still without an acting win. A victory would make him the oldest lead comedy actor champion ever, sailing past Eugene Levy, who was 73 when “Schitt’s Creek” swept in 2020. His competition includes a fellow member of the 0-fer club: Steve Carell, 64, whose pivot to the dark comedy “Rooster” brings his career acting ledger to 0-for-7 — six straight losses for “The Office,” one for “The Morning Show.” Will he ever win?
	



	

					Harrison Ford and Lukita Maxwell in “Shrinking,” now streaming on Apple TV.Season 3
									Apple TV
	



	The women’s races are just as historic. Sally Field, 79, returns to the limited series/TV movie field in the film adaptation of the acclaimed novel “Remarkably Bright Creatures,” finally getting the kind of showcase that may remind voters what she’s capable of. Her last Emmy came in 2007 for the ABC drama “Brothers and Sisters”; a win here would make her, by a matter of months, the oldest winner in the category’s history, something Kathy Bates missed last year with “Matlock.” Jessica Tandy was also 79 when she won for “Foxfire” in 1988.

	Youn Yuh-jung, 79, may have the best narrative in the entire field. Five years after becoming the first Korean performer to win an Oscar for “Minari” (2020), she earned her first Emmy nomination as the imperious Chairman Park in the second season of the anthology series “Beef.” A win would make her the first Korean actress to take a Primetime acting Emmy — Lee Jung-jae broke the barrier for the men with “Squid Game” in 2022 — and the first Korean performer to own both an Oscar and an Emmy for acting. She’d also join Eva Le Gallienne (1978) and Ellen Burstyn (2013) as only the third woman 79 or older to win the category.

	Michelle Pfeiffer, 68, finally gets the television vehicle worthy of her in Apple TV’s “Margo’s Got Money Troubles,” earning her second career nomination and positioning herself for a first Emmy that would double as a coronation for her small-screen era.

	And spare a cheer for Dale Dickey, 64, whose first nomination ever — supporting comedy actress for “Widow’s Bay” — arrives after four decades of being the best thing in everything from “Winter’s Bone” onward. That show, it should be said, is a veterans’ full-employment act all by itself.



	

					Perlah keeps an impatient Duke from leaving. (Warrick Page/HBOMAX)
									Warrick Page/HBO Max
	



	And then we have the lifers and character actors who are constantly referred to as “that guy” or “that gal.” Jeff Kober, 72, is having the kind of season character actors dream about: a guest drama nomination for his quietly devastating turn as the patient Duke on HBO Max’s medical drama “The Pitt,” paired with a Daytime Emmy nomination this year for revisiting “General Hospital” — the show that won him a Daytime trophy in 2022, for which he also self-submitted. Forty years after “China Beach” and “Sons of Anarchy” made him television’s most reliable menace, he’s on both Emmy ballots at once.
	

	Richard Jenkins, 79, nominated in supporting limited for “DTF St. Louis,” would become the second-oldest winner in his category’s history — behind only Paul Newman, who was 80 when he won for “Empire Falls” in 2005. There are worse men to follow.

	Which brings us to the nomination that will have the tear ducts full in the room. Rob Reiner, who was taken from us alongside his wife, Michele, in December at age 78, received a posthumous nod as guest comedy actor for his warm, funny arc as Albert, the franchising mentor in the fourth season of “The Bear.”

	The history here is almost unbearable. Reiner’s two Emmys came as Michael “Meathead” Stivic on the classic comedy “All in the Family,” the last of which was in 1978 — meaning a win would arrive 48 years later, the longest gap between acting victories in Emmy history. The man whose record he’d break would be his father. Carl Reiner famously waited 38 years between wins, from “Caesar’s Hour” in 1957 to “Mad About You” in 1995 — a victory that came in this very category.

	A posthumous win would also be the Emmys’ first for an on-camera performance since Raúl Julia in 1995 for “The Burning Season.” (Chadwick Boseman’s 2022 win was for voice work.)

	None of these wins are guaranteed.

	Emmy voters are not a sentimental bunch, and the categories are stacked and fiercely competitive. But with a veteran class that includes Ford and Field, Short and Root, Youn and Jenkins, Kober and Dickey — and Reiner above them all — the industry that spent decades treating its veterans as scenery would love to hand them their due on the big stage.

	On Sept. 14, somebody’s going to make history just by standing up.

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Sets Digital, 4K Blu-ray Release Dates

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is finally setting sail for home theaters.

	The blockbuster adaptation of Homer’s epic poem will be available to rent and purchase on digital beginning Nov. 17, following its theatrical debut on July 17. The film is also slated to arrive on 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray the same day.

	The digital release comes four months after Nolan’s nearly three-hour epic opened exclusively in theaters, marking a substantially longer theatrical window than most major studio releases. Nolan and Universal took a similar approach with “Oppenheimer,” which spent 123 days in theaters before arriving on premium video-on-demand and physical media in November 2023.


	The film has earned roughly $1.35 billion worldwide, making it Nolan’s highest-grossing movie and, as of this week, the highest-grossing R-rated film of all time, surpassing “Deadpool & Wolverine.” It has also grossed more than $500 million domestically. Imax has contributed a massive $257 million in ticket sales, and “The Odyssey” now ranks as the company’s highest-grossing release of all time.

	Matt Damon stars as Odysseus, the Greek king attempting to make his perilous journey home to Ithaca after the Trojan War. The sprawling ensemble also includes Tom Holland as Telemachus, Anne Hathaway as Penelope, Zendaya, Robert Pattinson and Charlize Theron. 

	In his review of the film, Variety’s Guy Lodge wrote that “There’s nary a dull moment in the director’s typically muscular, temporally complex interpretation.” 

	“But despite a fine, bone-weary turn from Damon as the wandering king of Ithaca,” he continued, “it’s more sensually than emotionally felt.”

title: ‘The Yogurt Shop Murders’ Crew Thought Their Journey Was Done Until There Was a Big Break in the Case: ‘We Have to Rally Now’
description: Two days’ notice is all director Margaret Brown had to figure out how to give her true-crime docuseries “The Yogurt Shop Murders” an ending. The ori
body: Two days’ notice is all director Margaret Brown had to figure out how to give her true-crime docuseries “The Yogurt Shop Murders” an ending. The original four-part series, chronicling the brutal 1991 murders of four young women in Austin, Texas, denied audiences what the victims’ families had similarly been robbed of for 35 years: closure.A killer had never been identified, and the four men some investigators believed were involved in the murders spent the last 20 years fighting the false accusations. It was hardly the kind of satisfying ending audiences often hope for in their true crime.But after the series aired on HBO last fall, Brown learned there had been a break in the case. She had two days to delay the planned start of another project and gather her crew to be on the ground when lead investigator Dan Jackson made the announcement that known serial killer Robert Brashers’ DNA had been linked to the crime. Brashers died by suicide in 1999, meaning families and friends finally had a name but not all the answers.“As soon as it was leaked, I called our producer Alice [Henty] and said, ‘We have to rally now,’” Brown says. “I turned back around and flew to Austin. That was on Saturday, and I think it was Monday we were shooting.”The lightning-fast regrouping to give this series an unexpected fifth chapter is the type of filmmaking feat that is often showered with awards, and “The Yogurt Shop Murders” was nominated for doc or nonfiction series. But historically speaking, it is an anomaly.Despite the true-crime craze that currently has a grip on streamers and networks, theseries is only the fifth murder-focused series to be nominated in the category in a decade, following “Making a Murderer” (2016), “The Keepers” (2017), “Tiger King” (2020) and “The Jinx Part 2” (2024).The category is constantly evolving. For years, exceptional nature and lifestyle documentaries like “Planet Earth” and “100 Foot Wave” dominated the nominee pool. But more recent years have seen it skew heavily toward celebrity-focused series, including three nominees this year for projects about Martin Scorsese, Sean “Diddy” Combs and Rafael Nadal. Other crime-centric series have made the cut over the years, like Investigation Discovery’s “Quiet on Set” in 2024 and Netflix’s “Wild Wild Country,” which won the statue in 2018. Yet, the tried-and-true-crime genre is often ignored, despite an endless library of options in any given year.“The Yogurt Shop Murders” is Brown’s first true-crime project, so she is hesitant to speak on why some of the most-watched docuseries each year are being overlooked by the Television Academy. But she does have an idea ­— or at least a hope — as to why her series, which counts Emma Stone among its producers, broke through where others haven’t.“It’s primal,” she says. “We all die. If you’re asking me, I really wanted to make something that touches on how people process grief in different ways and sneak it into the true-crime genre. Grief touches everybody, and it interests me that you can explore that with true crime. Can I make something that allows people to touch on their own experience with it through this genre?”Brown didn’t watch a bunch of true-crime classics before she took this story on. She didn’t try to hit on the hallmarks that define the genre, but she also knows that there’s great power in bringing attention and awareness to stories that may feel like local examples of tragedy, but can also offer universal insights into human nature.The impact of the series and the reach of true crime have been undeniable. While in Eastern Europe last year, she was in an Uber and the driver talked about the latest series she was watching ­— “The Yogurt Shop Murders.” It took some convincing, but the driver eventually believed she was carting around the director and immediately had questions. But that’s not even the most unexpected place Brown has found her own series.“It’s on Delta!” she says. “You don’t even know how many people are sending me photos from over someone’s shoulder, showing me that they’re watching it and crying on a plane.”One insight into the true-crime genre that Brown is still grappling with is the gendered reactions to it.“The way women respond to it has been really interesting to me,” she says. “A lot of my female friends are like, ‘I can’t watch that. I love you, but I can’t watch the show.’ Then some women are like, ‘Oh, my God, I have to watch all of it right away.’ Even I got so freaked out making this show that I got an alarm system installed, and I’ve never had an alarm system. There’s something about the story that just gets to you.”Could that be the barrier to entry for those in the Academy who simply don’t turn on true-crime docuseries? That people hesitate to even press play on these stories that might terrify them, or at least aren’t willing to admit they watched by throwing these projects their support?It’s a question that has plagued horror storytellers in television for decades and is currently being batted around with successes like “Widow’s Bay,” maybe thanks to the show’s comic element. But true crime still faces a split: It is by far one of the most bankable genres in Hollywood, even if the awards bodies in town don’t laud it as much as audiences.It’s unclear if “The Yogurt Shop Murders” is the first of many to come, or the last of the contenders to break through in an ever-changing category. But after descending into the genre for the series and then returning for its sudden ending, Brown can’t exactly blame those hesitant to do the same.“This is obviously really dark stuff, where I just don’t want to be in that world,” she says. “Life is too short, and I’d rather make a movie about dogs or crows or love or anything but death and rape.”

title: LISTEN: Amazon Courts Creators to Build Businesses and Scale the Attention Economy for Brands
description: On today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, Matt Sandler and Angie More of Amazon explain how the digital behemoth is diving in to
body:
On today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, Matt Sandler and Angie More of Amazon explain how the digital behemoth is diving in to the creator economy to build business and bring scale in ad buying to big brands. 

	Sandler, who is Amazon’s general manager of creator services, and More, head of creator ad partnerships, explain how they’re trying to leverage all that Amazon has to offer to support the new breed of digital stars. The company’s prime target are the born entrepreneurs who are launching products and businesses that are rooted in their success with social media-distributed content and the strength of their fan communities.
	

	“Over the last year, we’ve seen creators and the conversation around creators and media change dramatically. Creators used to be thought of in kind of more digital endemic terms. People who came up on YouTube or Twitch, and we saw that they started to shape culture. They started to shape how media was consumed. They started to shape how customers bought new things or selected products,” Sandler observes. “And so we took a look at creators more so as entrepreneurs. They are the center of gravity for their businesses, and most of those businesses are rooted in some form of content that could be a YouTube channel, that could be a Twitch livestream series, that could be a podcast, that could be a social series. But these entrepreneurs are rooted in content, and then they have extensions that expand well beyond the content and kind of the walls of any single platform.”


	The pair point to the burgeoning cottage industry around the Jason and Travis Kelce podcast “New Heights.” That show is the hub of a wheel that includes the Amazon-built e-commerce storefront Kelce Clubhouse, which sells a range of fan and lifestyle merch, not all of which is directly related to the sibling NFL players. The multifaceted Keke Palmer has also teamed with Amazon Creator Services for her “Baby, this is Keke Palmer” podcast that has led to other pacts in the Amazon-verse including Palmer’s plan to go live on Twitch twice a month.
	

	The array of options that creators pursue is part of the sizzle of the sector and something that greatly appeals to brands. Sandler and More’s work is to make it more adaptable and, yes, scalable for marketers.

	“What a lot of our advertisers are looking to us of like, how do you close the full loop of that customer journey throughout leveraging [Amazon’s] incredible creator suite and the connective tissue between a creator and their fan community,” More says. “We’re really working with brands and creators and tech and we’re really focused on telling that story and helping really shape where this industry goes from a measurement and impact perspective.”

	(Pictured: Amazon’s Matt Sandler and Angie More)

	“Strictly Business” is Variety’s weekly podcast featuring conversations with industry leaders about the business of media and entertainment. (Please click here to subscribe to our free newsletter.) New episodes debut every Wednesday and can be downloaded at Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, Spotify, Google Play, SoundCloud and more.

title: TikTok to Pay $400 Million to U.S. Government to Settle Lawsuit Alleging App Violated Child-Safety Law
description: TikTok, the company behind the popular short-form video app, has agreed to pay $400 million to settle a U.S. government lawsuit alleging that a pred
body:
TikTok, the company behind the popular short-form video app, has agreed to pay $400 million to settle a U.S. government lawsuit alleging that a predecessor app violated the country’s Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).

	The Justice Department announced the settlement with TikTok and China-based ByteDance on Friday. Under the terms of the agreement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately to the U.S. government and an additional $100 million “upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly,” the DOJ said. 
	

	The $400 million settlement represents one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a case involving COPPA, a law that requires websites and online services aimed at kids to obtain parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13.


	The lawsuit was filed during the Biden administration in August 2024, when the DOJ, together with the FTC, sued TikTok and ByteDance in California federal court, alleging that TikTok “knowingly permitted children to create regular TikTok accounts and to create, view and share short-form videos and messages with adults and others on the regular TikTok platform.” The DOJ alleged at the time that TikTok collected and retained a “wide variety of personal information from these children without notifying or obtaining consent from their parents.”

	Since the Justice Department filed the complaint in 2024, “TikTok has undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions and privacy practices,” the agency said in announcing the settlement. “The company has implemented extensive measures designed to strengthen safeguards for younger users, improve age-related controls, and enhance parental oversight. Those developments have materially advanced the public interests underlying the Department’s litigation and have strengthened protections for millions of American families.”
	

	In January 2026, under a deal brokered by the Trump administration, ByteDance sold a majority stake in TikTok’s U.S. business to non-Chinese investors, including Oracle, Silver Lake and Abu Dhabi’s state-owned investment firm MGX. Beijing-based ByteDance retains 19.9% of the joint venture; the deal brought ByteDance and TikTok into compliance with the U.S.’s TikTok divest-or-ban law that went into effect in January 2025.

	In a statement, U.S. Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. said: “This settlement is a major victory for American children and parents. The Department’s priority is ensuring that children are protected online and that companies entrusted with their personal information meet their legal obligations. This resolution secures a substantial recovery while reinforcing the protections that families expect and deserve.”

	Variety has reached out to TikTok and ByteDance for comment.

title: Shaquille O’Neal: Marvel Turned Me Down for the ‘Avengers’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Shaquille O’Neal will not be appearing in December’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” or any other “Avengers” film, for that matter.

	In an interview with Var
body:
Shaquille O’Neal will not be appearing in December’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” or any other “Avengers” film, for that matter.

	In an interview with Variety about his “Dunkman” league, the first professional dunking league where contestants from around the world compete for a grand prize of $500,000 — whose finals is airing the night of Aug. 25 on TNT — the NBA legend dished on his struggle to land roles in Hollywood where he doesn’t play himself.
	

	“I would love to do more action roles but we were told by top Hollywood executives that I’m too big, and what they mean by that is when I pop up on the screen everyone will go, ‘Oh, that’s Shaq!’ So, if I’m trying to play a doctor or anything, my character won’t be believable,” O’Neal explained.


	While O’Neal, 54, portrayed a DC superhero in 1997’s “Steel,” he says he’s spent years trying to be a part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe — namely, in an “Avengers” movie — but was rebuffed by the studio. He’d first made his desire to be in an “Avengers” movie known during a 2018 interview with EW.

	“I wanted to be in the ‘Avengers’ and they were like, ‘Shaq, we fuckin’ love you and we’d love to put you in, but if your face pops up on screen people are going to go, ‘Hey, that’s Shaq!’ He said it truthfully, and I was like, alright… I guess my face is too bigtime.”

	O’Neal did pop up in a fun cameo at the end of this year’s “Scary Movie,” and will also appear in “Grown Ups 3.” But now that the Marvel dream has died, he’s keen on sharing the silver screen with another hulking star, Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson.  
	

	“I want to do a movie with The Rock so I can beat him up,” he declares.  

	As for whether he can take down The Rock, Shaq replies, “Oh, easy! Barbecue chicken.”

	Variety’s full feature on Shaquille O’Neal and “Dunkman” will run Tuesday, Aug. 25.

title: Music Industry Moves: My Morning Jacket and Jim James Sign Publishing Deal With Peermusic
description: Peermusic has signed a worldwide publishing deal with My Morning Jacket and frontman Jim James, as announced by Jamie Cerreta, President of U.S. and
body:
Peermusic has signed a worldwide publishing deal with My Morning Jacket and frontman Jim James, as announced by Jamie Cerreta, President of U.S. and Canada. Through the deal, Peermusic will publish the go-forward works of My Morning Jacket as well as Jim James’ go-forward solo recordings, starting with his new album “Wowed Out,” due out August 28 on ATO Records. The deal marks a decades-long publishing relationship between My Morning Jacket, Jim James, and Cerreta, who first signed My Morning Jacket and Jim James to a publishing deal with Chrysalis in 2002.
	

	James said, “Since 2002, Jamie Cerreta and I have worked together building an incredible musical connection and friendship. He has always been such a wonderful guide and protector for all of the music I have created over the years, and I am so excited to join him and the rest of the family over at Peermusic!”


	Cerreta added, “I have been so lucky to work with Jim for most of my career. It has been a true honor to represent his amazing songwriting throughout the years. I couldn’t be more thrilled that he has joined up with what we are building at Peermusic.”

	+ SoundExchange has awarded MC Lyte with the SoundExchange Music Fairness Award. The honor recognizes the pioneering hip-hop artist’s legacy of advocacy, including her efforts to raise awareness, engage members of Congress, and urge passage of the American Music Fairness Act.

	Lyte was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2026 in the organization’s Early Influence category.

	In 2024, MC Lyte joined DMC (Run-DMC’s Darryl McDaniels) and Melle Mel to visit Capitol Hill to meet with key lawmakers about the American Music Fairness Act and urge its passage to compel corporate terrestrial radio broadcasters to pay performance royalties. She reengaged with legislators again this summer, visiting members of Congress to continue to press for passage of AMFA.
	

	“MC Lyte has spent her career breaking barriers, elevating artists, and using her voice to drive meaningful change,” said Michael Huppe, President and CEO of SoundExchange. “We are proud to honor her with the SoundExchange Music Fairness Award in recognition of her enduring leadership and advocacy for the creators whose work powers our culture.”

	“I am deeply grateful to SoundExchange for this recognition and for its unwavering commitment to standing up for artists,” said MC Lyte. “Advocacy has always been part of my purpose, and I believe that creators deserve to be respected, protected, and fairly compensated for the music and culture they bring to the world. I’m proud to stand with SoundExchange in the fight for music fairness and for a future where every artist’s work is valued.”

	+ 10th Street Entertainment management company has expanded with the official launch of the Pub Crawl Recordings label group and Pub Crawl Songs music publishing company. These new ventures will be an expansion on its current artist management division, dedicated to comprehensive artist development, curation, and maximizing creative IP.

	Leading this expansion, 10th Street Entertainment’s Chris Nilsson (President) and Lewis Kovac (COO) have appointed veteran music industry executive Piero Giramonti as Executive Vice President of Operations and Artist Manager. Giramonti brings decades of top-tier industry leadership to the role, having previously served as President of Sumerian Records and General Manager of Capitol Music Group’s Harvest Records and Caroline Independent Distribution.

	“I am so happy to be joining an organization with the pedigree of 10th Street Entertainment, where artists come first, and an incredible staff operate with passion, and with complete transparency and integrity,” says Giramonti. “I have known Lewis Kovac for 30 years. We have always had stellar success and great times working together. I have only recently gotten to know Chris Nilsson, but I can already see that he has passion, is thoughtful, calm, highly knowledgeable and very cool.”

	“Chris and I have always wanted to expand our company’s growth organically and we had the opportunity to reconnect with Piero at the right time,” says Kovac. “We share so many passions and our dedicated team is deserving of global scale to give our artists a world stage. Working with The Orchard is already smooth and they are excited to start releasing music.”
	

	Joining 10th Street’s Nashville office are Elizabeth Brahan Wright (VP of Music Publishing/Artist Manager), Clint Perry (Artist Manager) and Jim Prisco (Artist Manager).  The team manages the careers of Tyler Farr and Kanaan Brock, as well as Morgan Wade.

	+ Country artist Alison Nichols has signed a global publishing deal with BMG, expanding her relationship with the company where she is also signed as a recording artist with BBR Music Group/BMG Nashville. As an Asian-American artist in the country format, Nichols proudly describes herself as “half Korean, half redneck, and 100% American.”

	“Signing my first publishing deal is something I’ve dreamed about for a long time, and I’m so thankful to be doing it with the BMG family. Having people like Amy who believed in me and my songwriting from the very beginning makes this moment even more meaningful, and I can’t wait to see where this next chapter leads.”

	“We’re thrilled to continue building alongside Alison as she enters this next chapter of her career,” says Amy Scott,  Director, Creative BMG Publishing. “As both an artist and songwriter, she brings a rare combination of authenticity, passion and humor to everything she creates. Her ability to tell honest stories in a way that feels both deeply personal and universally relatable is what makes her such a special talent, and we’re excited to help champion her songwriting for years to come.”

	+ Electric Feel Publishing, part of Electric Feel Entertainment management, has signed the Elements (Keven Wolfsohn and Paul Bogumil Goller).The duo executive-produced Afrobeats superstar Ayra Starr’s new album, “Starr Girl,” and over the years have collaborated with Burna Boy, Pop Smoke, Rema, Wizkid, Central Cee, Zara Larsson, Lewis Capaldi and more.

	“We’re grateful to the EF team for their support and vision, and we’re excited to build the next chapter of our sound together. Music has always been about pushing boundaries and creating records that connect with people around the world. Joining Electric Feel Entertainment gives us an incredible team to help take that vision even further” said the Elements in a statement.

	“We’re excited to welcome The Elements to Electric Feel Publishing. Bogo and Kev have built an incredible track record and have become trusted collaborators for some of the biggest artists in the world. We’re looking forward to working with them and supporting what’s next,” said Austin Rosen, Founder & CEO of Electric Feel Entertainment.
	

	Tuesday, August 18 

	British rock band Wolf Alice has signed with UTA for touring representation in North America, the company announced on Tuesday.

	The signing comes as the quartet is slated to support Olivia Rodrigo on the first leg of her “The Unraveled Tour.” Kicking off on September 25, Wolf Alice will take to arenas across the U.S. over 18 sold-out dates. Earlier this month, the band performed at the Lollapalooza festival and played a sold-out show at New York City’s Pier 17. The band’s fourth and most recent studio album “The Clearing” was produced by Greg Kurstin (Adele, Paul McCartney, Pink, Foo Fighters), who won the Grammy producer of the year award two consecutive years.

	Monday, August 17

	RCS Worldwide has announced the promotion of Alissa Pollack to president of Mediabase, a top music industry source for airplay analytics, chart intelligence, and music data. In this elevated role, Pollack will also continue her full responsibilities as president of global music marketing at iHeartMedia.

	As president, Pollack will lead Mediabase’s strategic direction, global expansion, product innovation, and commercial growth, according to the announcement.

	Susan Larkin, RCS Worldwide president-CEO, said, “Alissa has spent her career at the intersection of music, data, and relationships, which is exactly where Mediabase lives. This promotion is a recognition of everything she has already built and a reflection of our confidence in where she will take Mediabase next. As she steps into this role she will have my full support as she leads Mediabase forward.”

	Pollack said, “I’m honored to lead Mediabase at such an exciting moment in its evolution while continuing the work I love at iHeartMedia. These roles are incredibly complementary because they share the same purpose: helping the industry make smarter decisions through meaningful insights.

	“As one of my first initiatives, I’m thrilled to make more Mediabase chart data publicly accessible through our newly updated Mediabase.com site. Music fans, industry professionals, and artists can now view the Top 50 charts across every format in both the U.S. and Canada, providing greater visibility into music performance and trends across North America.”

	+ Valerie Pensa, a multiple Clio Award winner who most recently was head of marketing at RCA Records, has left the company to launch of new venture Moonstruck Management & Marketing Inc., which is based in Los Angeles. Over the years she has worked closely with such artists as Tate McRae, P!nk, Doja Cat, Miley Cyrus, Sia, Lisa and more.
	

	Pensa said, “Moonstruck means dreamily entranced — devoted to something you believe in. That’s exactly how I feel about artists with real vision, and it’s the only way I know how to work. This industry doesn’t sit still and my job is to stay dedicated to that vision no matter how the business evolves.”

	+ Jet Management, the Venice, CA-based music management focused on dance music, has announced a new joint management partnership with Debonair (DBNR), the Belgium-based boutique music management company, launching with the acclaimed French electronic music duo Polo & Pan, who are currently on a North American tour as the support act for Jet Management act Empire of the Sun. DBNR’s roster also includes Charlotte de Witte, Enrico Sangiuliano, Bazart and Oliver Symons; Jet’s also manages Justice, Foster the PeopleSam Gellaitry, Neil Frances, WhoMadeWho and others; it is also a partner of the company Firebird.

	“I’ve been a longtime fan of Polo & Pan and genuinely enjoyed their records and live shows long before this collaboration came together,” said DBNR founder-CEO Alexander Vandriessche.  “We’ve always had a lot of respect for what Jet built and how they approach artists globally, and with Polo & Pan and this new partnership, there was a very organic fit between both teams and it felt like the right project to start building something together.”

	Jet co-founder Tyler Goldberg added, “We are thrilled for the opportunity to both work with one of the most creative and talented artists in the world, one which we’ve admired for years, and to partner with one of the best managers in our industry, our dear friend Alexander Vandriessche.”

	+ Mom+Pop Music has signed singer-songwriter Crash the Party. Signed by label co-founder Michael Goldstone and Katie Fagan, the artist has released the song “Cold Feet” to launch the partnership.

	Crash the Party says, “Growing up in rural Georgia, pursuing music sometimes felt a little delusional. I knew I wasn’t meant to work in a factory, lay cable, or follow the paths a lot of my neighbors took — I just knew I had to make music. Being with Mom+Pop is truly a dream, and it feels like validation that I’m on the right path, crazy or not!” More music will be released later in the fall.
	

	+  Fenix Entertainment has announced a global partnership with Maluma to lead the development and strategy behind his upcoming world tour, taking place in 2027 and 2028.The 35-year-old company currently works with Luis Miguel, Ricardo Arjona, and Ricardo Montaner, while also developing strategic partnerships with Shakira across multiple markets.

	Marcelo Fígoli, founder and president of Fenix Entertainment, said: “Working with an artist with Maluma’s career and international reach is both a challenge and an enormous responsibility. We believe in his vision, his talent, and the exciting moment he is experiencing in his career. We are incredibly proud to be part of this new chapter and to put our team and experience behind a project of this scale.”

	+ Warner Records Nashville has reshaped its marketing team structure with the announcement of several staff promotions and newly created roles:

	Addison Nunes is being promoted to VP of marketing where she will oversee marketing duties for one half of the roster alongside Anna Pittman, who will lead marketing efforts for one half as well, continuing her role as VP of marketing.

	Justin Luffman will move into the newly created role of VP of culture & creative marketing. In this role, he will act as a driving force behind our artists’ identities and cultural relevance, according to the announcement.

	Pittman will be supported by Jackson Ammons, who moves into his new role as marketing manager. Nunes is supported by new hire Jennipher Miller, who begins her new role as marketing manager, while Samantha Nepsa assumes Nunes’ previous duties with her promotion to senior analyst of data & analytics.

	Allyson Kim will move into the role of manager of touring & fan activations, while Alyssa Cohen joins the marketing team as coordinator, reporting to EVP of marketing Victoria Mason.

	+ United Talent Agency announced today the addition of six new executive appointments, along with 11 internal promotions across the music division. The announcement is the latest in a series of advancements for the department, including the recent elevation of James Wright to co-head of U.K. music, the announcement of seven new music partners in March, and the promotion of 19 colleagues in December.
	

	Chris Anderson (Agent), Randy Freedman (Agent, Music Brand Partnerships), Jordan Golenberg (Agent), and Lauren Katzakian (Executive, Business Affairs) are based out of Los Angeles. Anderson joins UTA following nearly two decades in artist management and talent representation. With over a decade of experience at Universal Music Group and elsewhere, Katzakian is the newest member of the UTA Business Affairs team focusing on touring and Music Brand Partnerships. Freedman also arrives via UMG, and will focus his efforts within the Music Brand Partnerships division. Golenberg joins from Day After Day Productions role.

	Anthony Brown (Agent) and Becky Drouet (Agent) join the ranks of agents in London. Brown brings over 13 years of industry experience from CAA, where he specialized in hip-hop and R&B. Drouet will work across touring and corporate/private group, following more than 18 years at LPO.

	UTA’s newest coordinator class will support agents and executives across several divisions within the music department, including touring, marketing, brand partnerships, music crossover, A&R and more. Juan Aguirre, Lindsey Cole, Alia Lopotanak and Mark Soleymani are the newest coordinators in the Los Angeles office; Julian Huff, Pearse Matteson, and Jenna Shatzman have been upped to coordinators in New York; Cat Ingersoll is the latest to be elevated to coordinator in Nashville; and Dylan Bryant, Brooke Newton and Emily Rhodes are the latest coordinator elevations in London.

title: ‘Novak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter’ Doc Director Unpacks the Tennis Champ’s Resilience and His Retirement
description: Novak Djokovic is, by the numbers, one of the best tennis players in the modern era. He has spent the most weeks — 428 — ranked as the world’s No. 1
body:
Novak Djokovic is, by the numbers, one of the best tennis players in the modern era. He has spent the most weeks — 428 — ranked as the world’s No. 1 player. He holds a record 24 Grand Slam singles titles, and he also has an Olympic gold medal. Djokovic emerged onto the tennis scene during the Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal era and won his first Slam in 2008 at the Australian Open when he defeated Federer. Suddenly, there was a new player in the race. He defeated Nadal in 2011 and reached No. 1 for the first time after winning Wimbledon that year. The “Big Three,” as they became known, dominated tennis, racing for majors and titles.
	

	As Djokovic continues to play and remain a force in the sport, one question surrounds him: When will he retire? “The Wolf in Winter,” directed by Jason Hehir, details Djokovic’s time to the very top of tennis. Now streaming on Prime Video, Djokovic is front and center. Hehir took time to reflect on why Djokovic is one of the greatest players and how he captured the tennis star behind-the-scenes in an attempt to humanize him.

	
		What made you want to tell Novak’s story?	

	As a huge sports fan, I knew that he was one of the most compelling characters in sports. I knew that he was controversial, outspoken, and polarizing. All of those things check the boxes for what makes an interesting documentary and a deep-dive character study. Novak is still dominating just about everybody — except for a couple of tennis players — at age 39, so I was really interested to see how he grappled with the notion that you can’t be the best dad in the world and the best tennis player in the world at the same time.
	
	
		People forget that you he lived in a war zone as a child, and it’s in the documentary where he recalls growing up during the bombings of Belgrade, and you know his wife is also, you know she talks about that. What was that like capturing that side of his childhood?	

	This film was never meant to be a definitive, comprehensive telling of his life story. I was interested in drilling down on the crossroads he finds himself at right now. That said, we needed to include some aspects of his backstory to inform viewers about why he’s making the decisions he’s making now and why he acts the way he does. He and his wife Jelena were clear about the fact that much of the behavior we see on the court — the outbursts, the anger, the passion, the emotion — is rooted in unresolved trauma from his childhood. He grew up in a war-torn country, routinely escaping to the basement of his apartment building to avoid NATO fighter jets and bombs overhead. He witnessed atrocious things as a kid. I believe that to this day, those experiences echo in his mind and inform the man he has become.
	
		Do you think that that added to his resilience? What did you learn about his resilience, or what drives that?	

	Novak is one of those athletes who, like a boxer, responds better when they’re punched in the face first. They need to be uncomfortable to excel. Andre Agassi said something similar in the film. When Novak is backed into a corner, that’s when he shines. He needs a wake-up call on the court to be his best, and that’s fueled his rivalry with Roger and Rafa. He wasn’t invited to their party. That was a two-man show—the perfect rivalry between two handsome, athletic stars adored by the tennis world. Then Novak comes along, with a name no one could pronounce, speaking a language no one recognized, from a war-torn country. I think that fueled his drive to equal them and, ultimately, eclipse them.
	
		I was surprised to see how pivotal a voice you made his wife Jelena be in this story. What made you want to use her to help tell the story?	

	It was clear to me that she is Novak’s rock, defending him more fiercely than anyone on the planet—including Novak himself at times. She has a deep, abiding love for him. She’s so articulate, intelligent, and curious, which made her a crucial voice in this story
	
	
		His retirement is such a tiring subject when he’s playing this well. How did you address approaching it with him?	

	I understand why he is sick of discussing retirement. If it was an anonymous player, and you didn’t tell me who it was and how old they were, you would never consider that this player might retire. You would say, “Oh, this player with the statistics they have and their results in Grand Slams, they must be one of the best players on earth.” And you’d be right if you said that. But then if you said it’s Novak Djokovic, he’s 39 years old. That’s when you say, “Okay, well, how long can you play? When is enough?” I understand why people ask the question the same way that I understand why he is sick of answering it. But we worked on this for over two years together, he pushed back on me a lot when it came to addressing retirement, I pushed back against him and said that it’s imperative for us to discuss this because that’s what’s being discussed when your name comes up, and I think you should take it as a compliment because it’s not that people are sick of you, and it’s not that you’re not performing well on the court and people are embarrassed for you. It’s that people are amazed that you’re still doing this at the level.
	
		What did you learn about the importance of family to to him?	

	Family matters more than anything to him, and and I’ve never seen anyone who loves a sport more than Novak loves tennis. But I think his love for family supersedes even that love. So, and that made it really interesting to see how he’s grappling with these two things that he adores, because he can’t give all of his time and attention to one of them when the other one is still there. There’s a scene when he’s recovering from the during the the Australian Open when he’s recovering from an injury, and he’s telling us that he can’t enjoy it anymore. in the moment, that’s how he felt. I think he probably, once he heals up and and gets some rest, he probably feels differently about that. But I felt it was really important to include that scene because that is how he felt in the that is some pretty incredible access that we’re getting to an elite athlete in a moment where he all of his resources are depleted, and he has to find some way to pick himself up off the ground mentally and physically, and and go out there and do it again in 24 hours.
	
	
		He’s one of the most misunderstood players in the sport, he’s polarizing. Can you talk about caputring that aspect in your storytelling?	

	Novak would rather be understood than loved. If 100% of people loved him but didn’t truly understand him, I don’t think he’d find that gratifying. He wants people to understand who he is, where he’s from, and why he acts the way he does. Then, people can take it or leave it. You can love him or hate him, but at least you understand him.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change in response to buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.

	Primetime Emmys Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: Aug. 21, 2026): Final Emmy voting begins Monday, Aug. 17, to determine who takes home statuettes over Labor Day weekend and then on the live telecast.

	HBO Max enters Phase 2 of the Emmy race as the most-nominated network, carrying the year’s two most-nominated series and a rare chance to capture television’s top drama and comedy prizes while potentially making history across all three major program categories.

	“The Pitt,” the sophomore season of the breakout medical drama, leads all programs with 25 nominations. Close behind is “Hacks,” which earned 24 to become the most nominated comedy series in Emmy history. The next closest is Apple TV’s horror-comedy “Widow’s Bay,” with 19.

	The platform’s current dominance marks its first time leading both genres since 2017.

	Few programmers in Emmy history have consistently produced the leading drama and comedy contenders in the same ceremony. History, however, shows that nomination dominance does not always translate into Emmy glory.

	Among the 18 instances in which a single network led the Emmy nominations in both drama and comedy, that network won one of the two top series prizes only four times (22%). By comparison, the most-nominated program series of the Emmy year has won its corresponding top category 41 times across 73 eligible ceremonies (56%). Last year delivered a rare exception when “Severance,” with 27 nominations, lost drama series to “The Pitt.” Before that upset, the most-nominated series had won its corresponding top category every year from 2015 through 2024.

	While “Hacks” leads the comedy field in nominations and already owns the comedy series trophy for its third season, the most-nominated comedy has historically converted at a lower rate than its drama counterpart.

	The most-nominated comedy series has won 25 out of 59 times in the current category format (42%). The front-runner has proved especially vulnerable in recent years, losing five of the past eight ceremonies, including 2023, when “The Bear” fell to “Hacks.”

	Also worth noting: the last comedy series to win in nonconsecutive years was “Everybody Loves Raymond,” which took the prize for its seventh season in 2003 and again for its ninth and final season in 2005, with “Arrested Development” winning in between. Other comedies to accomplish the feat include “Murphy Brown,” “Cheers,” “All in the Family” and, in the category’s earliest years, “The Jack Benny Show.”

	In limited series, HBO Max’s “DTF St. Louis” earned 13 nominations, including directing, writing and supporting acting recognition for David Harbour, Jason Bateman, Richard Jenkins, Linda Cardellini and Joy Sunday. The network hopes to overtake Netflix’s “Beef,” which leads the field with 16 nominations after its first installment won the category.

	“Beef” stars Oscar Isaac and Carey Mulligan appear well positioned in the lead acting categories, while Harbour and Cardellini face a more crowded supporting field because of their co-stars nominated from the same series. Charles Melton and Yuh-jung Youn, meanwhile, enter their respective races without internal competition. That absence of a same-series rival could prove valuable down the stretch.

	The limited series front-runner has been the least reliable of the three major program categories. The most-nominated limited series has won 16 of 45 times (36%), compared with 45% for drama and 42% for comedy.

	Since 2021, the nomination leader in limited series has lost four out of five times: “WandaVision” (2021), “Dahmer — Monster: The Jeffrey Dahmer Story” (2023), “True Detective: Night Country” (2024) and “The Penguin” (2025), which led with 23 nominations but lost to “Adolescence.” Only “The White Lotus” (2022) managed a victory.

	Winning the top series prizes in drama, comedy and limited series in the same year remains one of the rarest accomplishments in Emmy history. It has happened only three times: HBO achieved the feat in 2015 with “Game of Thrones,” “Veep” and “Olive Kitteridge,” while NBC accomplished it twice, in 1996 with “ER,” “Frasier” and “Gulliver’s Travels,” and in 1987 with “L.A. Law,” “The Golden Girls” and “A Year in the Life.”

	As always, the race is wide-open and subject to a few surprises. We’ll see which categories deliver just that.

	Final-round voting runs Aug. 17-26 ahead of the Creative Arts Emmy Awards and Governors Gala on Sept. 5-6. The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards will air Sept. 14 on NBC.

                          'You Are All That Matters To Me' ...
body:
Natalie Harp's Letters To Trump
                          'You Are All That Matters To Me' ...
                          'I Don’t Want To Ever Let You Down'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 21, 2026
                            2:41 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 21, 2026
                                10:30 AM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Natalie Harp penned intimate letters to President Trump ... and now we're seeing them for the first time, and they show Harp's total devotion to Trump, telling him he's all that matters to her and she never wants to let him down. 
      
    
            Trump's executive assistant wrote the 2 alleged letters to the president during or after his May 2023 golf outing at his courses in Scotland and Ireland. The Daily Beast published the letters in full Thursday night.
      
    
            In one letter, Harp apologizes to Trump, believing she may have upset him during their overseas trip. She wrote that she thought she was the only person left behind at the airport the night before, so she panicked and called Trump while alone in a van at Customs without her passport. She said she should have just contacted the Secret Service.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Harp also wrote she was sorry for stepping onto the golf course instead of riding in a cart. She pleaded with Trump to "please forgive me" if she had done anything else to cause him trouble.
      
    
            She went on to write that she wants "things to always be right between us" and that she's "been distracted all week" while forgetting to eat and sleep at times.
      
    
            In addition, Harp wrote that she feared Trump had a lower opinion of her after other people made remarks about her, noting that she only wants to bring joy to Trump. She then ended the letter by referring to Trump as “my Guardian and Protector in this life.”
      
    
                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            In the second letter, Harp thanked Trump for getting her to “unplug” while they enjoyed their time together on the golf course. She wrote, “We could be out on the Course, with no machines, and even forget what time it was! I didn’t have to be 'Human Printer'" ... referring to her nickname in the White House because she quickly prints out favorable Trump articles and hands them to the president.
      
    
            Harp also wrote she could see that Trump noticed her occasional “slightly negative” mood because she's rapidly approaching burnout. She wrote that she envied anyone whose job "seems to be to talk with [Trump] and look pretty," insisting, "I want that job!!”
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She also wrote that she feels like an "in-betweener" caught between Trump's staff and people who enjoy talking to him on the plane or at dinner. She said the experience harkens back to her days as a talk show host for the ultra-conservative "One America News Network," a job she says she hated.
      
    
            Harp wrapped up the second letter by telling Trump that he has the "absolute right to cuss me out, if need be, when I deserve it, because no one knows or cares about me more.”
